paper_title: ProAS: A Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping Framework for Multi-Turn Agentic Reinforcement Learning

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as the primary paradigm for optimizing Large Language Model (LLM) agents, yet efficient critic-free algorithms (e.g., GRPO) suffer from a fundamental uniform credit assignment dilemma that broadcasts trajectory-level advantages equally to all actions. Our analysis reveals that this uniformity inherently reinforces structurally unreasonable actions in preferred trajectories and ignores each action's downstream deviations in unpreferred ones. To resolve this without introducing critic overhead, we propose Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping (ProAS), a plug-and-play framework that leverages a dynamically evolving Agentic Reference Graph (ARG) to achieve fine-grained credit assignment via Masking Unreasonable Incentives (MUI) and Asymmetric Penalty Redistribution (APR). Extensive experiments across Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct demonstrate that ProAS universally elevates mainstream group-based baselines to new state-of-the-art performance, achieving peak success rates of 91.9% and 94.3% on ALFWorld, alongside 66.7% and 70.8% on WebShop, respectively. Furthermore, it accelerates training convergence by up to $2.44\times$ while maintaining strong robustness against imperfect or distilled ARGs. Codes: https://github.com/LINs-lab/ProAS

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents that make sequential decisions through interactions with external environments. Their planning and reasoning capabilities have enabled applications in software engineering (Yang et al., 2024), personal assistance (Yoran et al., 2024), and graphical user interface navigation (Luo et al., 2025). Reinforcement Learning (RL) has emerged as the primary paradigm for elevating the agentic capacity of LLMs (GLM-5-Team et al., 2026; DeepSeek-AI, 2026). During RL rollouts, agents generate trajectories composed of interleaved environment states and actions, which introduces fundamental credit assignment challenge: How should trajectory-level rewards and penalties be attributed to individual actions? Actor-critic algorithms (e.g., PPO (Schulman et al., 2017)) address this by learning separate critic, which introduces substantial computational overhead and optimization instability in long-horizon settings (Wang et al., 2026a; Yue et al., 2025). Conversely, critic-free algorithms like Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024) offer computational efficiency by broadcasting trajectory-level advantage uniformly to every action (Ding et al., 2025). To systematically understand the uniform credit assignment dilemma, we conduct fine-grained action-intervention analysis ( 4.2). Our findings reveal dual suboptimality. First, in preferred trajectories with positive advantages, uniform credit inadvertently reinforces structurally invalid actions (i.e., unreasonable actions) that pollute the context history and impede the agent from reaching success. Second, in unpreferred trajectories with negative advantages, uniform penalization ignores the autoregressive nature of LLMs, where the later deviations may drive from earlier actions. Consequently, they suppress all actions equally but arbitrarily without considering their actual downstream influence. To resolve this dilemma without introducing critic overhead, we propose Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping (ProAS) in 4.3. ProAS leverages an Agentic Reference Graph (ARG, mentioned in 4.1), which abstracts task progression into dynamically evolving sub-goals to formally annotate whether an action is reasonable (structurally valid) or progress-advancing (driving task completion). Using these structural annotations, ProAS asymmetrically reshapes trajectory-level advantages in Eq. 7: (1) Masking Unreasonable Incentives (MUI) zeros out the local advantages of unreasonable actions in preferred trajectories to prevent their inadvertent reinforcement. (2) Asymmetric Penalty Redistribution (APR) utilizes Future-Drift (Eq. 6), the inclusive count of downstream non-advancing actions, to assign proportionally heavier penalties to actions triggering severe downstream stagnation. Extensive experiments in 6 on ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2021) and WebShop (Yao et al., 2023) using Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (Qwen Team, 2024) validate ProAS as versatile, plug-and-play enhancer. It universally elevates mainstream group-based RL baselines (GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), DAPO (Yu et al., 2025), GiGPO (Feng et al., 2025)), boosting success rates by up to 16.7 points (e.g., GRPO on 1.5B ALFWorld) and accelerating training convergence by 1.12 to 2.44. On top of that, this orthogonal enhancement propels these standard algorithms to establish new state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance, consistently eclipsing the strong segment-level baseline, MiGPO (Wang et al., 2026b). Notably, GiGPO+ProAS outperforms MiGPO by massive 13.1 points on WebShop with 1.5B model and secures the highest overall success rate of 94.3% on ALFWorld with 7B model. Furthermore, comprehensive ablations ( 6.2) show that ProASs core mechanisms are both synergistic and superior to alternative advantage shaping variants, and confirm ProASs robust efficacy against incomplete or distilled ARGs, underscoring the necessity of ARGs online evolution mechanism. In summary, our primary contributions are: Problem Identification: We expose the uniform credit assignment dilemma in critic-free agentic RL, demonstrating how uniform advantages inadvertently reinforce contextual noise in preferred trajectories and ignore the downstream influence of actions in unpreferred ones. Algorithmic Innovation: We propose Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping (ProAS), plug-andplay framework. Guided by dynamically evolving Agentic Reference Graph (ARG), ProAS achieves fine-grained, critic-free credit assignment via Masking Unreasonable Incentives (MUI) and Asymmetric Penalty Redistribution (APR). Empirical Superiority: ProAS acts as universal enhancer across multiple model scales and environments. It significantly accelerates training convergence, propels standard group-based algorithms to surpass strong SOTA baselines (e.g., MiGPO), and exhibits high robustness against imperfect and distilled reference guidance.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORKS
sections.content: Multi-Turn Agentic Tasks. Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed to solve complex real-world tasks (Xu et al., 2025). Given the intricacies of these environments, agents must engage in multi-turn interactions, continuously accumulating contextual knowledge and making sequential decisions to drive task completion. To facilitate the training and evaluation of such agents, the community has introduced various simulated environments. Examples include ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2021) for embodied household tasks, WebShop (Yao et al., 2023) for web navigation, AppWorld (Trivedi et al., 2024) for application development, and τ 2-Bench (Barres et al., 2025) for evaluating dynamic conversational abilities in domains like aviation and retail.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Rather than constructing new environments, our work focuses on developing more efficient and effective training paradigms tailored for existing multi-turn agentic tasks. RL for LLM Agents. Critic-free RL like GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) is widely adopted for LLM agents (Qian et al., 2025; Jin et al., 2025; Wei et al., 2025), but suffers from sparse-reward advantage vanishment (Yu et al., 2025) and coarse trajectory-level credit assignment (Tan et al., 2026). While DAPO (Yu et al., 2025) and dense-reward methods (Qian et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026) mitigate this vanishment, their credit assignment remains trajectory-bound. To differentiate intra-trajectory actions, GiGPO (Feng et al., 2025) and MiGPO (Wang et al., 2026b) compute relative advantages by matching anchor states or milestones across rollouts. In this work, we systematically expose the flaws of uniform credit assignment in both preferred and unpreferred trajectories, addressing them through advantage shaping, which serves as plug-and-play module for existing critic-free RL algorithms.

sections.title: 4 METHODOLOGY
sections.content: Since RL fundamentally optimizes policies by incentivizing or suppressing action likelihoods, tailored credit assignment requires understanding both the intrinsic properties of each step (e.g., reasonableness and progress advancement) and how modulating them dictates the final outcome. To quantify these step-level properties, 4.1 constructs an Agentic Reference Graph (ARG). Guided by an intervention study probing these modulation effects ( 4.2), 4.3 introduces Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping (ProAS), lightweight framework designed to resolve the uniform credit dilemma via asymmetric advantage shaping. 4.1 AGENTIC REFERENCE GRAPH As illustrated in Fig. 1(a), ARG abstracts the task-solving progression into ordered sub-goals using pre-collected successful trajectories. Furthermore, while sub-goals follow strict sequence, their internal atomic requirements are often permutation-invariant (example in Appx. D.4). sections.title: 5 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
sections.content: To empirically validate the proposed ProAS framework, we conduct extensive experiments across complex, long-horizon agentic environments. Our experiments are structured to answer the following core research questions: RQ1: Performance & Efficiency ( 6). Can ProAS consistently elevate task success rates and accelerate training convergence across different model scales under different environments? RQ2: Algorithm Compatibility ( 6). Does ProAS seamlessly integrate with mainstream groupbased RL baselines (e.g., GRPO, DAPO, GiGPO) as robust plug-and-play module? RQ3: Advantage Shaping Design ( 6.2.1). Are MUI and APR each individually necessary and mutually synergistic, and does ProASs Future-Drift-based redistribution outperform simpler masking heuristic? RQ4: Robustness to ARG ( 6.2.2). Does ProAS remain effective when the reference ARG is randomized, incomplete, static (non-evolving), or distilled from teacher model? 5.1 MODELS AND DATA Models. Our experiments are conducted across two different model scales: Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (Qwen Team, 2024), which are denoted as 1.5B and 7B for brevity. Data. We train and validate on ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2021) and WebShop (Yao et al., 2023), two classical long-horizon multi-turn agentic environments (details in Appx. C). ALFWorld is text-based embodied benchmark over six household task categories (Pick, Look, Clean, Heat, Cool, Pick2, details in Table. 5). Our 150-step training comprises 1777/1767/1784 unique executable tasks of seed 0/1/2 for training and 128 for validation. WebShop  (Table 6)  is an HTML-based online shopping environment, with 2015/2011/2036 tasks of seed 0/1/2 used for training and 128 for validation.

sections.title: 5.1.1 EVALUATION METRICS
sections.content: Performance Metrics. For ALFWorld, we report the average Success Rate (SR) across the entire validation set, alongside the per-category average SR. For WebShop, we report both the overall average SR and the Task Score (TS). TS is checklist metric on scale of 0 to 100: it averages the satisfaction of the requested attributes, options, and price constraint, and then scales this score by how well the purchased product matches the requested product type. Efficiency Metrics. We quantify training efficiency via speedup Spd@K = NbaseK/NProASK, which is defined as the ratio of RL training steps required by the baseline versus ProAS to first reach target of SR. sections.title: IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
sections.content: We conduct experiments upon Verl-Agent (Feng et al., 2025), training all models for 150 RL steps. We validate the policy every 10 RL steps and report metrics from the checkpoint achieving the highest SR. Unless otherwise specified, all experiments are conducted across three random seeds (0, 1, and 2), reporting the mean and sample standard deviation (std). See details in Appx. B. ARG Initialization. Unless otherwise specified, we initialize the ARG in ALFWorld using its official crowdsourced annotations. Given the strictly sequential nature of tasks in ALFWorld, we formulate each individual step as distinct sub-goal. For WebShop, the ARG is initialized using its officially annotated sub-goals alongside their corresponding states and actions. 5.1.3 BASELINES We consider baselines of different paradigms: (1) Proprietary models: GPT-5.6-Sol (OpenAI, 2026), the state-of-the-art model from OpenAI. We apply the reasoning effort as high, and evaluate it with ReAct prompting (Yao et al., 2022). (2) Prompting: Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7BInstruct, the starting point to be trained. (3) Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT): Tuning the agent by imitating curated turn-level oracle trajectories from the same training tasks as RL baselines (Details in Appx. B.3). (4) RL: the classical actor-crtic algorithm PPO (Schulman et al., 2017); mainstream group-based RL algorithms GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), DAPO (Yu et al., 2025), GiGPO (Feng et al., 2025); the state-of-the-art (SOTA) agentic RL method MiGPO (Wang et al., 2026b) with segment-level credit assignment.

sections.title: 6 RESULTS AND ANALYSIS
sections.content: 6.1 MAIN RESULTS Table 1 summarizes the main evaluation results on ALFWorld and WebShop. We structure our analysis to directly address our research questions regarding performance, efficiency (RQ1), and algorithm compatibility (RQ2). Baseline Comparisons. We first contrast ProAS against established learning paradigms. While both SFT and ProAS leverage expert annotations as supervisory signals, ProAS abstracts them into ARGs to structurally guide RL, significantly outperforming SFTs direct behavior imitation. Specifically, GiGPO+ProAS achieves 91.9% and 94.3% SR on the 1.5B and 7B ALFWorld benchmarks, respectively, surpassing SFT by 12.2 and 14.4 points. Furthermore, ProAS consistently eclipses PPO, conventional critic-based RL algorithm, across all settings. ProAS variants outpace PPO by 5.5 to 18.7 points in ALFWorld SR, alongside steady improvements of 4.1 to 12.2 points in WebShop TS and 3.4 to 11.5 points in WebShop SR. Ultimately, these results confirm that explicitly integrating ARG-derived progress signals into RL is vastly superior to both passive trajectory imitation and conventional critic-based credit assignment. State-of-the-Art Performance. Equipped with ProAS, group-based RL algorithms consistently establish new SOTA records. In ALFWorld, GiGPO+ProAS attains the highest SR of 94.3% on the 7B model. This surpasses the strong segment-level baseline MiGPO and eclipses the proprietary GPT-5.6-Sol by massive 15.4 points. Crucially, ProAS demonstrates remarkable plug-and-play compatibility, universally uplifting baseline RL algorithms across all tested configurations. For ALFWorld, equipping GRPO with ProAS yields the most dramatic improvements, boosting the SR by 16.7 points on the 1.5B model and 8.4 points on the 7B model. Consistent gains are mirrored in WebShop, where DAPO+ProAS generates 9.4-point uplift at the 1.5B scale, and GRPO+ProAS provides 3.1-point boost at 7B. This confirms ProAS as versatile enhancer that elevates both the performance floor and ceiling of diverse group-based RL paradigms. Training Efficiency. Beyond asymptotic performance, ProAS significantly accelerates the training process. On average, it speeds up convergence to target success rates by approximately 1.5 for the 1.5B model across both environments. Impressively, this efficiency gain scales favorably with model size: on the 7B model, ProAS accelerates learning by an average of 2.2 on ALFWorld and 1.7 on WebShop. 6.2 ABLATION STUDY We ablate the core components of ProAS on the 1.5B model using GRPO as the base algorithm. 6.2.1 ablates our advantage shaping mechanisms, demonstrating that disabling any single technique lowers the overall success rate and disrupts their synergy. Subsequently, 6.2.2 relaxes the ARG construction constraints to investigate ProASs robustness against reference quality and origin, while highlighting the critical necessity of the online dynamic evolution mechanism. 6.2.1 ADVANTAGE SHAPING ABLATION To isolate the contributions of our specific advantage shaping interventions, we evaluate five ProAS variants: PR (Progress-aware Reward), ProAS, ProAS+, ProASmsk and ProASsuffix, as shown in Table 2(a).

sections.title: 7 CONCLUSION
sections.content: In this work, we expose the uniform credit assignment dilemma in critic-free agentic RL, where uniform advantages reinforce contextual noise in preferred trajectories (Ai > 0) and ignore the downstream deviation of actions in unpreferred ones (Ai < 0). To address this without critic overhead, we proposed Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping (ProAS), which leverages dynamically evolving Agentic Reference Graph (ARG) to achieve fine-grained credit assignment via Masking Unreasonable Incentives (MUI) and Asymmetric Penalty Redistribution (APR). Extensive evaluations across multiple model scales and environments confirm ProAS as robust, universal enhancer that accelerates convergence and propels mainstream baselines to new state-of-the-art performance. The ablation study further confirms MUI-APR synergy, necessity of ARG evolution and robustness under incomplete or distilled ARGs. Together, these results establish highly efficient, scalable pathway for elevating autonomous language agents.

sections.content: B.1 TRAINING FRAMEWORK For ALFWorld and WebShop, we adopt the Verl-Agent (Feng et al., 2025) framework. To ensure robustness and reproducibility, we sample and freeze three distinct training sets with environment seeds 0, 1, and 2 for independent and repeated training. For fair evaluation, all resulting model checkpoints are assessed on unified, static validation set of 128 tasks. This validation set is strictly

RL and SFT share the same turn-level input format illustrated in Tables 11 and 12: each prompt contains the task instruction, current observation, admissible actions, and the visible interaction history from the two most recent observation-action turns. The only difference between SFT and RL data is the assistant response, which is curated offline for SFT but generated online for RL. All experiments are conducted on GPUs. For ALFWorld and WebShop, each 1.5B model run uses 2 GPUs, while each 7B model run uses 4 GPUs. B.2 RL CONFIGURATION General. We follow the standard Verl-Agent (Feng et al., 2025) configuration and use the same settings across all RL methods unless otherwise specified. Models are optimized with AdamW using learning rate of 106, weight decay 0.01, and gradient clipping at 1.0. We use PPO clipping ratio of 0.2, an entropy coefficient of 0.001, KL-loss coefficient of 0.01, and one policy-update epoch per rollout batch. At each RL iteration, we sample 16 prompts and generate = 8 trajectories per prompt with temperature 1.0 and top-p = 1.0. For ALFWorld, we set the maximum prompt and response lengths to 2,048 and 512 tokens, respectively, cap each episode at 50 steps, and use PPO mini-batch size of 256. For WebShop, the corresponding settings are 4,096 prompt tokens, 512 response tokens, 15 steps, and PPO mini-batch size of 64. Reward. Across all runs, we use the same rule-based sparse outcome reward Ro in both environments: successful trajectory receives 10, whereas an unsuccessful trajectory receives 0. To construct controlled imitation-learning baseline matching the RL methods task exposure, we curate supervised dataset for each environment seed (0, 1, 2) from the frozen training tasks: ALFWorld: We execute the official annotated expert trajectory to obtain one demonstration per unique training game. WebShop: Lacking official experts, we instantiate deterministic, goal-conditioned oracle from our ARG using task metadata (target product, query, and options). The resulting trajectories strictly follow the ARGs sub-goal progression (g1 g6, details in Table 10), explicitly grounding the demonstrations in the same progress structure used by ProAS. Aligning with the data setting in RL experiments. we represent SFT data as turn-level examples rather than complete trajectories. Each input contains the task instruction, current observation, admissible actions, and the two most recent interaction turns. Table 11 and Table 12 demonstrate the SFT data example of ALFWorld and WebShop. Training Configuration. We perform full-parameter fine-tuning of Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with the SFT trainer based on FSDP in Verl-Agent, minimizing the token-level negative log-likelihood of the oracle responses. We train for 3 epochs with AdamW (β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.95), peak learning rate of 105, weight decay of 0.01, and gradient clipping at 1.0. The learning rate follows cosine schedule with 3% warmup. We use maximum sequence length of 4,096 tokens with left truncation and per-GPU micro-batch sizes of 4 and 2 for the 1.5B and 7B models, respectively. We save the checkpoint at the end of each epoch and evaluate every epoch checkpoint on the same frozen 128-task validation set used for RL. The SFT result is reported from the checkpoint with the highest validation success rate.

sections.title: D CASE STUDY
sections.content: D.1 UNREASONABLE ACTION PROBING ANALYSIS IN ALFWORLD We compare two visible-history conditions while fixing the underlying environment state and rollout budget. Both conditions replay the same three-action clean prefix and reach the same continuation point: the agent is at desk 1, holding keychain 2, with 47 steps remaining. From this state, we independently sample 50 continuations {ci}50 i=1 under each condition. In the noise-injected condition, four unreasonable actions are prepended only to the policy-visible interaction history; they are not executed in the continuation environment and therefore do not alter its starting state. Table 7 first presents the task ARG and then traces the clean and noise-injected conditions separately. Only the four injected unreasonable actions are highlighted in pink. The sampled suffixes are summarized by continuation row, followed by the Expected Success Rate (ESR) for each condition. The two panels therefore differ only in the pink history segment; their clean prefix, continuation state, and rollout budget are identical. The observed ESR decrease from 82% to 58% thus diagnoses the effect of unreasonable content in the policy-visible history rather than change in the underlying environment state. D.2 VARYING FUTURE-DRIFT ACTIONS SUPPRESSION ANALYSIS IN ALFWORLD We examine the suppression of four non-advancing actions from the same 50-step failed ALFWorld rollout in Table 8 (c), which are actions of steps 3, 28, 40, and 47. At each position, we preserve the complete preceding prefix, reject only an exact match to the original action, and independently sample 50 continuations {ci} i=1. The intervention results exhibit monotonic relation in this case: the ESR is 24%, 16%, 10%, and 0% when suppressing actions with FD 47, 23, 11, and 4, respectively. The larger recovery at higher-FD positions supports Future-Drift as diagnostic proxy for an actions downstream failure burden. Because the four decisions occur at different prefixes and remaining horizons, this case is intended as direct intervention evidence for the diagnostic trend rather than standalone estimate of universal causal effect. D.3 THE ARG DYNAMIC EVOLUTION IN ALFWORLD Table 9 illustrates the online ARG evolution mechanism using the task Look at pencil under the desk lamp. Because the environments success criterion broadly accepts any pencil index (e.g., pencil 1 or pencil 2), the task inherently possesses multiple valid solutions that single static ARG fails to cover. To capture this diversity, any rollout verified as successful during training is first purified by pruning invalid and inadmissible steps. The retained valid path is then seamlessly merged into the current ARG, dynamically expanding its coverage of viable solution trajectories. D.4 THE ORDER-AGNOSTIC OF ACTIONS IN WEBSHOP Table 10 shows WebShop case from Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct GRPO rollouts. The task-level ARG is ordered across sub-goals, but its option-configuration sub-goal g3 contains an unordered set of required options. partial g3 state satisfies one required option, while g3 is completed only after all required options are selected. The price and attribute constraints, g4 and g5, are checked at purchase time before the trajectory reaches g6. The contrast highlights the intended granularity of action annotations deriving from ARG. Trajectories and differ only within g3: they visit different intermediate option states but reach the same completion-state equivalence class, so both option orders are treated as progress-advancing. Trajectory shows the complementary cases: wrong option and premature purchase are unsupported by the ARG, whereas repeated click on an already selected option can be reasonable but non-advancing. Thus, the ARG preserves ordering constraints among high-level sub-goals while avoiding spurious penalties for valid option permutations.
